blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Part III (Articles 12–35) covers Fundamental Rights guaranteed under the Indian Constitution.
Writ jurisdiction is conferred on the Supreme Court via Article 32 and High Courts via Article 226.
Directive Principles of State Policy are enumerated in Part IV (Articles 36–51).
Fundamental Duties were added under Part IVA (Article 51A).
Article 368 governs the power and procedure for Constitutional Amendments.

blocks.content: The Constitution of India came into force on 26 January 1950. It was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 (Constitution Day). Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee. The original Constitution had 395 Articles, 8 Schedules, and 22 Parts. Currently it has 470 Articles, 12 Schedules, and 25 Parts (after amendments).

cells: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar — Father of the Indian Constitution
Sir B.N. Rau (Constitutional Adviser to Constituent Assembly)
Declared India a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic; Socialist and Secular added by 42nd Amendment, 1976
India has the longest written constitution in the world

blocks.content: The Preamble declares India to be a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic and secures to all citizens: Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith, and worship), Equality (of status and opportunity), and Fraternity (assuring dignity of individual and unity and integrity of the Nation).
Important: The Preamble is not enforceable in court (Berubari Case, 1960) but it is part of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati Case, 1973). It is a key to interpret the Constitution.

cells: Equality before law (Art.14); Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth (Art.15); Equality of opportunity in public employment (Art.16); Abolition of Untouchability (Art.17); Abolition of titles (Art.18)

Six freedoms under Art.19 (speech & expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession); Protection against arbitrary arrest; Personal liberty (Art.21); Protection against double jeopardy, self-incrimination (Art.20)
Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour (Art.23); Prohibition of child labour in factories/hazardous employment below 14 years (Art.24)
Freedom of conscience and religion (Art.25); Freedom to manage religious affairs (Art.26); No tax for promotion of any religion (Art.27); No religious instruction in State-funded schools (Art.28)
Protection of interests of minorities (Art.29); Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions (Art.30)
Dr. Ambedkar called this the 'Heart and Soul' of the Constitution; Right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights; Writs
Release illegally detained/imprisoned person; most important for personal liberty
Direct to perform a public/official duty it is legally bound to perform but has refused
Prevent inferior court from exceeding its jurisdiction; issued before final order
Quash order of inferior court made in excess of jurisdiction or against natural justice; after final order
Inquire into legality of a person's claim to hold a public office

blocks.content: Important: High Courts can issue writs for any purpose (Art.226), not just enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Supreme Court issues writs only for enforcement of FRs (Art.32).
1.4 Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV — Articles 36–51)
DPSPs are non-justiciable (not enforceable by courts) guidelines for the State in making policies and laws. They represent social and economic democracy. Inspired by Irish Constitution.

cells: Social order for welfare; equal pay for equal work (Art.39d); right to work, education, public assistance (Art.41); just and humane conditions of work (Art.42); living wage (Art.43); workers' participation in management (Art.43A)
Village Panchayats (Art.40); cottage industries (Art.43); cooperative societies (Art.43B); promotion of SC/ST interests (Art.46); prohibition of intoxicants (Art.47); cow protection (Art.48)

Uniform Civil Code (Art.44); free and compulsory education — now FR under Art.21A (Art.45); protect environment (Art.48A); protect monuments (Art.49); separation of judiciary from executive (Art.50); international peace (Art.51)

blocks.content: Important: Fundamental Rights vs DPSPs: In case of conflict, FRs generally prevail. But 42nd Amendment gave primacy to certain DPSPs. Minerva Mills Case (1980) restored balance.

Added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976 based on Swaran Singh Committee recommendations. Originally 10 duties; 11th added by 86th Amendment, 2002 (duty of parents/guardians to provide education to children aged 6–14).
1.6 Union and Its Territory (Part I — Articles 1–4)

cells: India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States; territory includes States, UTs, and acquired territories
Parliament may admit new States or establish new States by law
Parliament can form new States, alter boundaries, names — simple majority; not under Art.368
Such laws are not Constitutional amendments under Art.368
Permanent body; 1/3 retire every 2 years; member serves 6 years
Introduced only in Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha can only delay by 14 days
Confidence motion; no-confidence motion against Council of Ministers
Can authorise Parliament to legislate on State List (Art.249); can create new All India Services (Art.312)
Art.108: President can call joint sitting for deadlock (not for Money Bill or Constitutional Amendment Bills)

items: Elected indirectly by elected members of Parliament and State Legislative Assemblies
5-year term; eligible for re-election; can be removed by impeachment (Art.61)
Art.74: Council of Ministers headed by PM to aid and advise the President — advice is binding
Ordinance-making power (Art.123): when Parliament not in session; must be laid before Parliament; lapses after 6 weeks of reassembly
Pocket veto — President can withhold assent indefinitely for non-Money Bills (Giani Zail Singh precedent)
Comparing Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Court) writ powers is frequently tested in exams.
Questions often ask for matching Constitutional Parts (Part I, III, IV, IVA, VI) with their corresponding Article ranges.
Article 123 (Ordinance-making power of the President) and Article 368 (Constitutional Amendments) are key targets for direct questions.

cells: Original (disputes between states/Centre-State); Appellate (civil, criminal, constitutional); Advisory (Art.143); Writ (Art.32)
